# Partition of India: Why India was divided in 1947 

The partition of India took place in 1947 and marked the end of British colonial rule.

It saw the country divided into two independent countries; India and Pakistan. The new border ran through villages and towns, through families and religious sites. 

In the months following the announcement, the country witnessed one of the largest mass migrations in human history. Since 1947, several wars have been fought over this border, and tensions still exist today between these two nuclear-armed neighbours. 

If partition was destined to be so disastrous, why did it happen? Who made this decision? And how did it go so wrong?

Dr Yasmin Khan, professor of modern history at the University of Oxford, explores the history of partition in this video, filmed at IWM London.

With thanks to Andrew Whitehead and his interviewees from the project Partition Voices, for the testimonies heard in this video. 

## Why was India partitioned? 

 View video transcript Hide video transcript 

### Transcript

Voiceover: "In the summer of 1947 two lines were drawn on a map; India and Pakistan. A message was broadcast across the British Empire: Independence of India within the next few months; the nation was to be divided. The new border ran through villages and towns, through families and religious sites. In the months following the announcement, the country witnessed one of the largest mass migrations in human history, and some of the worst violence of the bloody 20th century. Since 1947, several wars have been fought over this border, and tensions still exist today between these two nuclear-armed neighbours. But if partition was destined to be so disastrous, why did it happen? Who made the decision? And how did it go so wrong? 

Partition marked the end of the British colonial rule of India – the jewel in the Empire’s crown. The British had begun trading with India in the early 1600s, when the East India Company was set up as a trading organisation. But over the next few centuries, the East India Company grew increasingly influential in the country, and by the mid-1700s, it had assumed control. In 1857, a rebellion against the company broke out. In its aftermath, the East India Company was dissolved, and the British Crown took direct control under the governance of the British Raj. But a desire to be free from British rule continued to grow and discontent swelled."

Dr Yasmin Khan, professor of modern history, University of Oxford: "So India had an independence movement from the very start of the 20th century. And there were all sorts of leaders who were involved in campaigning for home rule. That was different to Independence - it just meant that people wanted democracy within the confines of the British Empire. After the First World War, though, this home rule movement really took off and escalated under the leadership of Mahatma Gandhi and he turned what was an elite movement into one of mass participation with huge demonstrations, public marches, and all kinds of people, from peasants to townspeople getting involved in the nationalist movement."

Voiceover: "The Indian National Congress had been formed in 1885 as a nationalist party promoting equality for Indians. Gandhi joined the National Congress in 1915 and he quickly became a proponent of anti-colonial peaceful resistance. Alongside the movement for independence from British rule, there was growing discontent among the religious communities in India. In the early 20th century, Muslims accounted for around 23% of the population, some 68% were Hindu, and around 2% were Sikh. Many Muslims and Hindus at the turn of the 20th century were dissatisfied with the Indian National Congress. There was great concern that it represented Hindu interests at the expense of other religious groups, and also that its secularism would not protect religious communities. In 1906 the All-India Muslim League was founded, the first political party for Muslims in India. Alongside this, a Hindu nationalist movement was growing. In 1915, the Hindu Mahasabha was founded. Then, in 1925, the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh organisation, with the single aim of uniting and strengthening India’s Hindu community. Mohammad Ali Jinnah joined the Muslim League in 1913. Initially he was opposed to the idea of a separate Muslim state and advocated for unity, but he would later play a crucial role in pushing for two nations."

Dr Yasmin Khan: "There were concentrations in Punjab and Bengal but there were Muslim minorities everywhere. And so this created a real demographic issue, a real numbers problem, which is how did you represent those people and make sure that their interests were represented in any new constitution, without conceding too much to those groups disproportionately and making sure that they felt culturally, economically, politically represented in the new nation state. I should also say that the divides were definitely not just along religious lines. There were many areas where Muslims and Hindus would have more in common than not because of the language that they spoke, because of the culture locally. So looking at it in, say, the early part of the 20th century, I think people would have been really shocked or surprised to imagine a subcontinent that would be divided up with these borders that were created in 1947."

Voiceover: "The British Indian Army fought in the First World War as part of the British Empire, with more than a million troops serving oversees. After the war, independence calls grew louder. In 1919, a large protest was organised against the extension of repressive wartime measures. British troops reacted by firing on the unarmed protesters in what has became known as the Jallianwala Bagh massacre, killing hundreds. The event led to Gandhi’s non-cooperation movement as well as Gandhi’s arrest. When he was released in 1924, relations between Hindus and Muslims had deteriorated. Furthermore, legislation imposed by the British Raj was cementing the religious divisions."

Dr Yasmin Khan: "During the time that they expand, the British tended to use different groups and castes for different jobs. For instance, recruit heavily from one community as policemen in an area where they might have been a minority in order to police the majority. And that happened in a state like, the United Provinces or to Pradesh, where the majority of policemen were Muslim even though they were in a minority. And this was a classic imperial tactic. It was a way of ensuring loyalty and deploying people in a way which drew on their caste or religious affiliation. Now, there were other ways that the British, also, looked at this diverse subcontinent and thought the defining characteristic here is religion. And so for that reason, when local councils and municipal councils were being set up, it was granted on religious lines. So the electorates were separate. You could only vote for a Muslim representative if you were a Muslim. And this clearly channelled politics along religious lines."

Voiceover: "Over the next few decades, revolutionary movements gathered momentum across the country. Gandhi continued to lead high profile protests such as the Salt March in 1930, and many tens of thousands of people were arrested. Local elections in 1936 saw the National Congress win significantly across the country, but the Muslim League failed to establish a government in any province, leading to furthers divisions. Then in 1939, Britain declared that India was at war with Germany. The Congress Party had not been consulted on the decision. This move and the ensuing impact of the war, sounded the death knell for British rule in India."

Dr Yasmin Khan: "So, the Second World War was a massive event in India, and we forget that now. But India was really caught up in the Second World War. Once Japan swept into Southeast Asia and into Burma, India was really on the front lines. 2.5 million soldiers joining the Indian Army, and that was a volunteer army. And the war also affected inflation; prices went sky high very quickly, and food scarcity was an issue for all sorts of people across the subcontinent, not only in the devastating Bengal famine of 1943, which killed 3 million people. But all throughout the subcontinent, people were going hungry. Inflation and the cost of goods in cities and towns in particular were rising. So the war had multiple effects on India and I think a lot of historians are starting to really recognise how important socially and economically the Second World War was for shaping what happened in 1947, just two years after the end of the war." Voiceover: "In 1940, under the leadership of Mohammed Ali Jinnah, the Muslim League called for a separate state for Muslims – it became known as the Lahore Resolution. Their belief was that no plans put forward by the British would be beneficial to Muslims in India unless the Muslim-majority areas of India were grouped into independent states. There was in fact a large contingent of the Muslim authority who opposed the idea of a separate Muslim state – led by the All-India Azad Muslim Conference, but their voice over time was muted. Gandhi was opposed to all forms of violence including war. He and the other leaders of National Congress saw Britain’s exploitation of India for the war effort without consulting them as morally wrong. In August 1942, Gandhi delivered his "Quit India" speech, demanding full and immediate independence for India. Across the country people joined in the movement."

Dr Yasmin Khan: "Wartime really exacerbated differences between the Muslim League and the Indian National Congress. One of the reasons for that was because the key leaders of the Indian National Congress were in prison for most of the Second World War. So Jawaharlal Nehru, who was the leader of the Indian National Congress along with Gandhi. Gandhi himself was imprisoned and fasted. They were only released just before the end of the war in the summer of 1945. And what that meant was that the Muslim League, which had been quite a small and not particularly successful party, was able to leap ahead. And when it came to elections at the end of the second World War, which were kind of a referendum on whether Pakistan should happen, the Muslim League boosted their support massively and won all the votes that they needed in a way, which was very surprising and shocking for lots of people."

Voiceover: "The war left Britain with severe economic problems, and the civil unrest in India was a growing concern. Independence for India now seemed inevitable. Britain's new Labour government under Clement Attlee was elected in 1945, and they pledged to end British colonial rule of India. The end of the Second World War also saw a series of mutinies, culminating in the mutiny of the Royal Indian Navy in Bombay in February 1946. The British government was compelled to act fast. The Cabinet Mission was formed, and sent to India to begin discussions with Hindu and Muslim leaders."

Dr Yasmin Khan: "The key players were the Congress and the Muslim League. But there were other parties involved, the princes who were the, the royal leaders and also other representatives were very important. Ambedkar, who was the leader of the, the untouchables, so-called the Dalits, the lowest in the pecking order of the caste system. So, there were lots of different people involved and all trying to make their voices heard. And the at the sort of centre of this were the British government, the viceroy, and the government back in London trying to work out an ideal settlement that would get the best kind of deal, both for South Asians, but really for Britain, too."

Collections footage voiceover: "Unassumingly they tackle the biggest political problem in the world. God guide them."
